A.title: UK Commission to Test Case for a New Gambling Act
A.excerpt: A new independent Gambling Policy Commission will ask whether the 2005 Act still works. Evidence closes 12 February 2027.
body: A newly formed independent body, the Gambling Policy Commission, has opened a wide-ranging review of whether Great Britain's Gambling Act 2005 remains fit for purpose or should be replaced. Reported on 9 November 2026, the review is chaired by Professor Jagjit Chadha of the University of Cambridge, with Professor James Reade of the University of Reading as chief economist, and draws on economists, lawyers, public-policy specialists and people with sport and regulation experience. The call for evidence closes on 12 February 2027, evidence gathering and commissioned research will run through 2027, and a final report is planned for 2028.

The timing reflects the age of the framework. The 2005 Act is more than twenty years old, and the last comprehensive independent review was about twenty-five years ago. The Commission is also asked to assess whether the reforms set out in the 2023 Gambling White Paper have produced measurable results and were proportionate and evidence-based. For licensed operators that is a notable shift in posture: the question is no longer only what the Gambling Commission will do next, but whether the statutory architecture beneath it should be rebuilt.

The remit is unusually broad on products and technology. The Commission will consider whether current rules can cope with prediction markets, artificial intelligence, cryptocurrencies and gambling-like features in digital products, and where gambling meets financial activity, including how regulators should handle cross-sector products. Given the volume of litigation and regulatory activity on event contracts elsewhere, any recommendation on the perimeter between gambling and financial services could have commercial consequences well beyond Great Britain.

Tax and economics feature prominently. The terms of reference refer to the effect of recent duty changes on operators and consumers and the interaction between tax and the statutory research, prevention and treatment levy. They record that Machine Games Duty rose from 5% to 25% at the Autumn Budget, that DCMS estimates gambling added about 5 billion pounds of gross value added in 2024 and supported around 75,000 jobs in 2025, and that HMRC recorded 3.9 billion pounds of betting and gaming duties in 2025/26. Readers should verify the duty figures against official sources, but the direction of travel is plain: the cost-benefit case for the sector will be reopened.

Several questions go to the structure of the licensing system itself. The Commission will examine whether some remote gaming should remain under commercial licences or move to restricted licensing or public provision, whether future law should allow civil liability for gambling harm, whether sports should hold economic rights over betting on their events, and whether part of General Betting Duty should become a statutory Sports Betting Levy, with British horseracing a particular focus. Each is a potential change to the commercial bargain between operators, sport, government and consumers, and each will attract organised lobbying.

Illicit gambling is the counterweight to every proposal for higher cost or tighter control. The review will look at the scale of offshore and unlicensed activity, why consumers use it, and enforcement across payments, websites, search, social media and app stores. A Gambling Commission survey cited in the terms of reference found that 2.5% of online gamblers had used an illegal site in the previous four weeks. Expect operators to argue that duty and affordability policy should be tested against channelisation, while campaigners argue that the licensed market is itself the source of harm.

For operators, the practical step is to treat the call for evidence as a strategic filing rather than a consultation response. Positions on liability, levy design, licence categories and product boundaries should be developed with specialist counsel, supported by data, and aligned with trade-body submissions where interests coincide. UK gambling practices such as Harris Hagan, Wiggin and Mishcon de Reya regularly advise on regulatory strategy and policy engagement. This article summarises public reporting and is not legal advice; check the Commission's published terms of reference before relying on any date or figure.

A.title: Brazil's STF Hears Betting Ban Evidence: What Comes Next
A.excerpt: Brazil's Supreme Court heard 26 institutions on the betting ban on 3 November. Operators now await a ruling and a congressional vote.
body: On 3 November 2026 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (STF) held a public hearing on Provisional Measure 1.394/2026, the instrument that banned fixed-odds betting and ended operators' authorisations. Justice Luiz Fux, rapporteur of ADI 8027, called the hearing, which heard from 26 institutions including government bodies, football clubs, industry groups and researchers. A public hearing gathers evidence and does not decide the case, but it shows which arguments the Court regards as material and how the government intends to defend the measure.

The government's case was framed as constitutional duty. Attorney General Jorge Messias argued that regulation had not delivered the protection the Constitution requires and that the state must act when safeguards prove insufficient. Health Minister Alexandre Padilha cited household debt, mental-health harm and organised crime, and said that 28 million Brazilians had bet in the previous twelve months, of whom 10.9 million showed risky or problem behaviour. Abras, the supermarkets association, reported that food sales rose 6.5% in the week of 5 to 11 October and 6.3% the following week compared with 2025, which the government side presented as evidence of reallocated household spending.

Football bodies emphasised the economic cost. Flamengo estimated annual losses of R$430 million and Fluminense R$200 million, while Vitória said betting contracts worth R$45 million represented about 17% of its revenue. The CBF said the ban had halted sponsorship talks for 2027 to 2030 and could cost R$420 million next year. Clubs and operators also made the policy argument that prohibition pushes players to unlicensed sites and that stronger enforcement of the licensed regime would protect consumers better than a ban.

The legal challenges are numerous. Four direct actions are directed at the measure itself: ADIs 8024, 8027, 8028 and 8035. Three earlier actions, ADIs 7721, 7723 and 7749, challenge the 2023 Betting Law (Law 14.790/2023), and the Court will also consider evidence from a November 2024 hearing at which more than 50 experts spoke over two days. The new issues include legal certainty, non-retroactivity, legitimate expectations, and whether the constitutional requirements of relevance and urgency for a provisional measure were met.

Those last arguments are where lawyers for licensed operators are likely to concentrate. A provisional measure is an executive instrument with force of law that must be converted by Congress, and its use is constrained by the requirement of urgency. Cancelling authorisations granted under a statute that Congress passed only in 2023, without compensation, invites arguments about acquired rights and the protection of legitimate expectations, even if the Court accepts that gambling policy is within the state's police powers. The outcome may turn on whether the Court treats the measure as a regulatory change or as an expropriation of lawfully acquired positions.

The procedural path matters for planning. The STF must still rule on the challenges, and Congress must vote on the measure for it to become permanent law, with no specific deadline for either set out in the reporting. Until then licensed betting remains offline across Brazil, and recent reports show that executive and judicial authorities have so far prevailed over individual operators seeking interim relief. Operators should assume that no relief will arrive quickly and plan for a lengthy period without Brazilian revenue.

Practical steps follow. Operators and suppliers should maintain a record of Brazilian licence fees, grant payments, investments and contractual commitments to support any future compensation or constitutional argument, and should review force majeure, termination and indemnity provisions in sponsorship and platform agreements. Brazilian specialists such as Pinheiro Neto Advogados and Mattos Filho are following the ADIs and the congressional process. This article summarises public reporting of the hearing and is not legal advice; confirm the status of each action with Brazilian counsel.

A.title: Norway Consults on State-Run Online Poker
A.excerpt: Norway proposes giving Norsk Tipping exclusive online poker rights, with strict loss limits. Consultation closes 29 November 2026.
body: Norway's Ministry of Culture and Equality published a consultation on 29 September 2026 proposing that Norsk Tipping hold the exclusive right to offer online poker, limited to tournament poker and cash games. No operator can legally offer online poker in Norway today. The consultation closes on 29 November 2026, so interested parties have a little under three weeks to respond. The proposal follows the Norwegian model of channelling gambling through state-owned and non-profit operators rather than licensing private companies.

The draft includes some of the most restrictive player-protection parameters in the European market. Loss limits would be NOK 5,000 per day and NOK 10,000 per month, reduced to NOK 2,000 per month for players under 20, and players could use at most four tables at once. The ministry is also asking whether poker marketing should be banned altogether. Those parameters would define the product: a limit of NOK 10,000 per month is far below the stakes at which many regular players currently play on international sites.

The rationale is channelisation. A 2022 University of Bergen survey found that nearly 90,000 Norwegians play online poker with foreign operators each year. The ministry's position is that those players currently receive none of the protection Norwegian law gives to residents of other games, and that a regulated offer, even with low limits, would give the state a way to apply consumer-protection controls. The difficulty, which respondents will press, is that very low limits may not be attractive enough to draw players away from foreign sites.

For international operators the proposal confirms that Norway will not open to private licensing. The consultation therefore matters less as a market-entry opportunity than as a signal of how Norwegian regulators will treat unlicensed offers. Norway has taken a firm approach to unlicensed operators in recent years, including payment-blocking and enforcement against marketing, and a poker monopoly would give the authorities a legal basis to treat poker offers by foreign operators as unlawful, which they currently cannot do by reference to a specific poker prohibition.

EU and EEA law is the underlying legal question. Monopoly models can be justified where they are consistent and systematically pursue objectives such as the prevention of gambling harm, and the loss limits and table caps in the draft are designed to support that justification. Respondents, particularly poker operators and player associations, may argue that the limits are disproportionate or that the case for a monopoly is weaker where an activity is currently unlawful and there is no existing domestic offer. How the final proposal answers those points will determine its resilience in any EEA challenge.

Suppliers, affiliates and payment providers should also note the marketing question. A ban on poker marketing would affect operator-brand sponsorship, streaming and content relationships, particularly where poker content is distributed in Norway from abroad. Businesses with Norwegian audiences should review whether current practice would continue to be lawful if a poker monopoly is introduced and whether contractual terms with partners address regulatory change.

Responses are due by 29 November 2026, and advisers with clients in the poker supply chain should consider whether to file individually or through a trade body. Firms such as Bird & Bird and CMS advise on Nordic gambling regulation and EEA law. This article summarises public reporting of the consultation and is not legal advice; check the consultation text before relying on any figure.

A.title: Morocco and Jamaica Tighten Casino Oversight
A.excerpt: Morocco's AML inspections of seven casinos and Jamaica's illegal-gambling warning show emerging-market regulators raising their game.
body: Two developments in early November 2026 show how emerging gambling jurisdictions are building supervision. In Morocco, a report published on 2 November covering the 2026 financial year described anti-money-laundering inspections of all seven operating casinos. In Jamaica, the Casino Gaming Commission used Illegal Gambling Awareness Week, 9 to 13 November, to warn the public that no licensed casinos are yet operating. Both illustrate the same regulatory shift: from legislation on paper to supervisory activity that operators and advisers need to understand.

Morocco's report, coordinated by the Interior Ministry with the Ministry of Economy and Finance, records inspections carried out in April 2026 of seven casinos: three in Agadir, two in Marrakech and one each in El Jadida and Tangier, on the figures reported. Compliance reviews were also carried out of three operators, SGLN (the national lottery company), SOREC (the horse-racing society) and MDJS (the games and sports company). The checks covered suspicious transaction reporting, customer due diligence, identification of beneficial owners and ongoing monitoring of business relationships, along with transaction-monitoring systems at the operators.

The legal basis is Morocco's anti-money-laundering framework, including Law No. 43.05 and amendments to the Criminal Code under Law No. 12.18. The report does not say whether any casino or operator breached the rules, and it identifies no penalties, licence suspensions or corrective measures. That absence is itself informative. At this stage the regulator is demonstrating coverage and building a supervisory record, and the first enforcement outcomes will show how strictly the rules are applied. Training workshops for casino staff on national law and international AML and counter-terrorist-financing standards suggest the approach is educational first.

Jamaica is at an earlier stage. The Casino Gaming Act permits casino gaming only under a licence from the Commission, and Adamas Grand Casino Limited holds the country's first Casino Operator's Licence, with the first licensed casino expected to open in 2027. The Commission, whose CEO is Cleveland Allen, has set up a framework that allows casinos to be licensed as part of approved integrated resort developments. Its warning is that live-dealer blackjack, roulette and baccarat offered for money in bars, lounges, clubs and private rooms are unlicensed and illegal, and that players at such tables have no guarantee of fair games and no regulator to turn to.

The Jamaican position also shows a limit of the regime. The Commission says its legislation does not allow it to take enforcement action against illegal casino-style operators and that it can only pass reports to law enforcement. That is a structural gap that investors and licensed operators will want addressed, because a licensed casino carrying the cost of regulation competes with unlicensed tables that carry none. Expect advocacy for amendments giving the Commission direct enforcement powers before the first licensed property opens.

Several lessons follow for operators and their advisers. First, AML and beneficial-ownership controls are now routine inspection topics even in markets that have only recently regulated, and operators should expect to be asked for evidence rather than policies. Second, early licensees often face uneven enforcement against illegal competitors, which should be reflected in business plans and in discussions with regulators. Third, regulators in smaller jurisdictions increasingly participate in international bodies and conferences, such as the IAGR meeting in Lima in October, and borrow standards from larger regimes.

Offshore and international practices such as Appleby and CMS advise on gambling licensing and AML compliance across multiple jurisdictions. Operators considering Jamaica or North African markets should obtain local advice on licensing routes, suitability requirements and enforcement. This article summarises public reporting and is not legal advice.

A.title: Brazil's Betting Ban: Licence Fees and the 120-Day Clock
A.excerpt: Operators that paid R$30m for Brazilian licences get no refund under the ban. The measure also lapses unless Congress acts within 120 days.
body: Brazil's Provisional Measure 1.394, signed by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on 25 September 2026, banned fixed-odds betting, including sports betting and online casino games. New deposits stopped the same day, players could withdraw until 5 October, and licensed sites went offline on 6 October. Authorisations end 30 days after publication, and the R$30 million licence fees paid by operators are not refunded. For market-entry strategy, Brazil has moved in under a year from the world's most closely watched new licensing regime to a closed market.

Two legal clocks now run in parallel. A provisional measure is an executive act with immediate effect, but it lapses unless Congress approves it within 120 days. Reporting on the measure notes that it will expire if Congress does not act, which gives lawmakers and the industry a defined window in which political conditions can change. Separately, the Supreme Federal Court is hearing several constitutional challenges, so the final shape of the policy may be set by judges as much as by legislators.

The financial exposure is already visible in listed groups. Entain had expected Brazil to account for about 5% of its online net gaming revenue in its 2026 financial year and now expects results near the lower end of its 910 to 960 million pound EBITDA guidance. Allwyn, which owns 36.75% of Kaizen Gaming, said that Brazil is Betano's largest market. For private operators and suppliers the position is harder to read, but the pattern of fixed licence fees, grant payments and local compliance investment with no revenue to offset them is the same.

The question for counsel is what remedies exist. The measure's text, as reported, excludes refunds or compensation, so any recovery would need to be won through constitutional litigation, contractual claims against counterparties, or political settlement. The legitimate-expectations arguments before the Supreme Court are the most direct route, and some operators may also consider investor-state protections where corporate structures and bilateral investment treaties allow. Those routes are slow and uncertain, and the strength of each depends on how the licence was acquired, the entity that paid, and the relevant treaty definitions.

Illicit-market risk is the other consequence. Bet Legal, run by Iron Security, counted 981 unauthorised betting domains at the end of 28 September, up from 377 on the day of the ban. Operators that exit lawfully, while unlicensed sites remain accessible, lose customers to competitors that do not comply with Brazilian law. Industry representatives made this argument to the Supreme Court. For compliance teams, it also creates a reputational point: suppliers, affiliates and payment partners must make sure they are not working with sites that continue to serve Brazilian players.

Contract and corporate decisions are pressing. Sponsorship, affiliate, platform and payment contracts should be reviewed for termination, suspension and force majeure provisions, and for obligations that survive licence revocation, including player-fund reconciliation and data retention. Group finance teams should consider impairment and disclosure obligations, and boards should record the basis of decisions to continue, restructure or exit Brazilian operations. Brazilian-law advice is essential, since many clauses will be tested for the first time.

Market entry elsewhere should take note. Brazil's experience demonstrates the regulatory-change risk that attaches to any new regime, particularly when fees are paid up front and political support is fragile. Diligence for new markets should include analysis of the instrument that created the regime, the ease with which it can be reversed, and any compensation protections. Firms such as Pinheiro Neto Advogados and Mattos Filho are advising on the Brazilian position. This article summarises public reporting and is not legal advice.
